findings.title: Infinite-loop hang: procedure body missing "end procedure" followed by an outer "begin" spins the parser forever
findings.description: parse_procedure_body()'s statement loop is `while (Current_parse_token_type != T_END)`. If a statement fails and the current token is already T_BEGIN (e.g. the procedure never got its own `end procedure` and the very next keyword in the source is the enclosing scope's `begin`), the code calls resync_parser(S_PROCEDURE_BODY). Inside resync_parser's first switch, the S_PROCEDURE_BODY case immediately matches `Current_parse_token_type == T_BEGIN` and does `new_state = original_state; break;` WITHOUT consuming any token (parser.cpp:2775-2779). The corresponding second-switch `case S_PROCEDURE_BODY:` (parser.cpp:3132-3135) is an empty no-op that also consumes nothing. Control returns to the caller with the token stream completely unchanged, so the outer `while (Current_parse_token_type != T_END)` loop calls parse_base_statement() on the exact same T_BEGIN token again, forever. Confirmed empirically: a minimal program with a procedure missing `end procedure;` before the program's own `begin` causes `./compiler` to hang and spin at ~100% CPU (verified via `timeout 3 ./compiler ...` -> exit 124, and `ps` showing the compiler process at 102% CPU while stuck).
findings.evidence:
parser.cpp:609 `while (Current_parse_token_type != T_END) { valid_parse = parse_base_statement(); ... valid_parse = resync_parser(state); ...}`; parser.cpp:2775-2779 `if (Current_parse_token_type == T_BEGIN) { new_state = original_state; break; }` (no token consumed); parser.cpp:3132-3135 `case S_PROCEDURE_BODY: break;` (no-op). Repro file used: `program test is
procedure foo : integer ()
begin
    return 0;
begin
    y := 1;
end program.
` -> `timeout 3 ./compiler minimal_hang_test.src` returned exit 124 and the child process was observed at 102% CPU via `ps -eo pid,ppid,pcpu,cmd`.

findings.title: resync_parser reads/returns the uninitialized locals new_state and return_state (undefined behavior), confirmed to reach the default: branch on real input
findings.description: resync_parser declares `parser_state new_state;` and `bool return_state;` (parser.cpp:2625-2627) with no initializer. The first switch's while-loops for S_PROGRAM_BODY (2646), S_PROCEDURE_BODY (2771), S_IF_STATEMENT (2916) and S_LOOP_STATEMENT (2956) can each exit their loop (loop condition becomes false, e.g. current token becomes T_SEMICOLON or T_INVALID) without ever executing a `new_state = ...;` assignment -- for S_IF_STATEMENT/S_LOOP_STATEMENT this happens whenever the panic-mode scan reaches a semicolon without first matching IF/FOR/RETURN/END/IDENTIFIER. The subsequent `switch (new_state)` (line 3046) then reads this uninitialized value, and if it doesn't correspond to one of the branches that assigns `return_state`, the final `return return_state;` (line 3286) also returns an uninitialized bool. g++ -O2 -Wall -Wextra flags both reads as `-Wmaybe-uninitialized`. This was also observed to fire on real (malformed) input: parsing a procedure whose closing is malformed prints "Error in resync start state" (the `default:` branch, parser.cpp:3281-3283) twice, which can only be reached if `new_state` held a garbage value not matching a real parser_state.
findings.evidence:
parser.cpp:2625-2627 `bool return_state; parser_state new_state;` (uninitialized); parser.cpp:3046 `switch (new_state)`; parser.cpp:3286 `return return_state;`. g++ -O2 -Wall -Wextra -c parser.cpp output: `parser.cpp:3046:5: warning: 'new_state' may be used uninitialized [-Wmaybe-uninitialized]` and `parser.cpp:3286:12: warning: 'return_state' may be used uninitialized [-Wmaybe-uninitialized]`. Empirical trigger: compiling `program test is
procedure foo : integer ()
begin
    return 0;
end program.
` (missing `procedure` keyword after `end`) printed `Error in resync start state` twice before the final error report.

findings.title: Global-scope updates silently discard the caller's new mutation: global variables/procedures never get identifer_type persisted, global arrays never get is_array persisted
findings.description: SymbolTable::update_identifier_type(token token_to_update, int scope_id) is used by the parser to persist identifier-kind/array-usage mutations (e.g. Current_parse_token.identifer_type = I_VARIABLE / I_PROCEDURE before declaring, and identifier_token.is_array = true when an identifier is indexed). When the identifier is already present in the global (-1) pseudo-scope, the function does `token_to_update = get_globabl_token(token_to_update); token_to_update.scope_id = scope_id;` -- i.e. it throws away the caller's freshly mutated token and replaces it with whatever was PREVIOUSLY stored in scope_table[-1], only patching scope_id, before resyncing. Any new field the caller just set (identifer_type, is_array) is lost. Verified with instrumented builds: (1) `global variable myglobal : integer;` leaves scope_table[-1].scope_map["myglobal"].identifer_type == 0 (I_NONE) instead of I_VARIABLE(2); (2) `global procedure myproc ...` leaves its global identifer_type at 0 (I_NONE) instead of I_PROCEDURE(1); (3) `global variable arr : integer[10]; ... arr[2] := 5;` leaves scope_table[-1].scope_map["arr"].is_array == false, whereas an equivalent non-global array declared/used the same way in scope 0 correctly ends up with is_array == true (control test) -- proving the loss is specific to the global-scope short-circuit branch.

findings.title: Declaring a local variable with the same name as an existing global variable corrupts the global variable's recorded data type instead of creating an independent shadow, violating the spec's global-name-uniqueness/shadowing rule
findings.description: SymbolTable::update_identifier_data_type(identifier_name, data_type, scope_id), reached from parse_type_mark(variable_name, 2) during any `variable <id> : <type>` declaration, checks token_is_in_global_scope(...) by NAME ONLY (not by whether the current declaration is itself global). If a name already exists in the global (-1) scope, it fetches the ACTUAL GLOBAL TOKEN, mutates ITS identifier_data_type field to the new local declaration's type, sets scope_id to the local scope, and then resync_tables (because global_scope==true on the fetched token) writes it back into scope_table[-1] too -- overwriting the global entry's type with the local declaration's type. Confirmed empirically: `global variable x : float;` followed by a nested `procedure foo() variable x : integer; ...` changes scope_table[-1].scope_map["x"].identifier_data_type from FLOAT(2) to INT(1) after parsing (verified via a control run without the nested shadow, which correctly leaves it at FLOAT(2)). Spec2023.txt explicitly states: 'Global names must be unique. Local names (procedures or variables) can be reused in other procedures. Local names can also shadow (or overload) a global name' -- implying a local declaration should not mutate the global entry at all; this implementation does the opposite.

findings.title: No duplicate/re-declaration detection anywhere; re-declaring a global name with a different type is silently accepted, contradicting the spec's global-uniqueness rule
findings.description: The parser never emits any 'already declared' / 'duplicate' / 'redeclaration' diagnostic anywhere (grep of parser.cpp for those terms only turns up comments). Each of the four declaration-handling functions (parse_procedure_header, both parse_variable_declaration overloads, parse_type_declaration) has an explicit empty branch when a name being re-declared as global is already global: `else { }` with the comment 'can we redefine global?' -- i.e. the code acknowledges the question and answers it by doing nothing (no error, no rejection). Confirmed empirically: `global variable x : integer; global variable x : float;` parses with 'The program parsed successfully with no errors', silently letting the second declaration win (and per finding above, actually corrupting/overwriting the type). This contradicts spec2023.txt's explicit rule 'Global names must be unique.'

findings.title: Copy-paste bug: declaring a bool variable records data type TYPE_INT instead of TYPE_BOOL in the symbol table
findings.description: In parse_type_mark(std::string identifier_name, int context) -- the overload used for ordinary (non-parameter) variable declarations via parse_variable_declaration(bool)'s call `parse_type_mark(variable_name, 2)` at parser.cpp:1282, and for procedure return types at context==1 -- the T_BOOL_TYPE branch's `context == 2` case calls `Lexer->symbol_table.update_identifier_data_type(identifier_name, TYPE_INT, current_scope_id);` instead of `TYPE_BOOL`. Every `variable <id> : bool;` declaration (outside of procedure parameters, which go through the correct 3-arg overload at parser.cpp:1064-1069) is recorded in the symbol table as having data type TYPE_INT rather than TYPE_BOOL, corrupting downstream type information for every non-parameter bool variable in the program.
findings.evidence: parser.cpp:888-905 `else if (Current_parse_token_type == T_BOOL_TYPE) { ... if (context == 2) { Lexer->symbol_table.update_identifier_data_type(identifier_name, TYPE_INT, current_scope_id); } ... }` -- contrast with the correctly-written T_INTEGER_TYPE/T_FLOAT_TYPE/T_STRING_TYPE branches immediately above it (parser.cpp:845-847, 863-865, 881-883) which each pass their own matching TYPE_* constant. The parameter-context 3-arg overload correctly uses TYPE_BOOL at parser.cpp:1069.

findings.title: Array bound is parsed but never recorded; declared identifiers are never marked as arrays at declaration time, so there is effectively no array-bound validation
findings.description: In both parse_variable_declaration overloads (parser.cpp:1238-1316 and 1319-1395), the optional `[ <bound> ]` is parsed via parse_bound()/parse_number() (parser.cpp:1289, 1368) purely to validate that a number token is present; the resulting value is discarded (parse_number never stores intValue/floatValue back onto the declared identifier, and the `token` struct (token.h) has no bound/array-size field at all). Neither overload ever sets `is_array = true` on the declared identifier's symbol-table entry. `is_array` is instead set ad hoc at USE sites only (parse_assignment_destination at parser.cpp:1957 and parse_name at parser.cpp:2510), unconditionally, regardless of whether the identifier was actually declared with a bound -- so a scalar variable indexed with `[...]` is marked 'array' just as readily as a real array, and (per a separate finding above) that use-site marking is itself lost for global identifiers. Net effect: the parser performs no real array-bound/array-usage validation; the declared bound size is entirely unused after being syntax-checked.
findings.evidence: parser.cpp:1286-1301 `if (Current_parse_token_type == T_LBRACKET) { Current_parse_token = Get_Valid_Token(); valid_parse = parse_bound(); if (Current_parse_token_type == T_RBRACKET) {...} }` -- no symbol-table write of is_array or a size anywhere in this block or in parse_bound() (parser.cpp:1399-1411) or parse_number() (parser.cpp:1541-1569). token.h:128 shows only `bool is_array = false;` with no bound/size field. Confirmed via instrumented run: after `global variable arr : integer[10];` followed by `arr[2] := 5;`, scope_table[-1].scope_map["arr"].is_array printed as 0 (never became true).

findings.title: update_scopes(false) is skipped (scope leak) when a procedure's closing 'end procedure' is malformed
findings.description:
parse_procedure_body() only calls update_scopes(false) (which decrements current_scope_id/number_of_scopes and removes the scope table) inside the branch where Current_parse_token_type == T_PROCEDURE is confirmed immediately after consuming a T_END token (parser.cpp:664-669). If the closing sequence is malformed -- e.g. 'end' is present but not immediately followed by the keyword 'procedure' -- the else branch (parser.cpp:670-675) just reports an error and calls resync_parser without ever calling update_scopes(false), permanently leaving current_scope_id/number_of_scopes incremented for the remainder of the parse. Confirmed empirically: parsing `program test is
procedure foo : integer ()
begin
    return 0;
end program.
` (missing the `procedure` keyword after `end`) leaves current_scope_id == 1 and number_of_scopes == 1 at the very end of the whole program's parse (should be back to 0), meaning any subsequent scope-based symbol lookups in the rest of the file would be evaluated against the wrong (leaked) scope id.
findings.evidence: parser.cpp:654-675 `if (Current_parse_token_type == T_END) {...} else {...} if (Current_parse_token_type == T_PROCEDURE) { update_scopes(false); ... } else { generate_error_report(...); valid_parse = resync_parser(state); }` -- no call to update_scopes(false) in the else branch. Instrumented run of the malformed-closing test printed `DEBUG final current_scope_id=1 number_of_scopes=1` at the end of parsing (program had only this single top-level procedure and no further nested scopes).

findings.title: Implementation accepts declaration/type-mark forms (type declarations, enum, identifier-as-type-mark) that are absent from spec2023.txt's grammar
findings.description: spec2023.txt's <declaration> production (grammar lines ~42-46) is only `[global] procedure_declaration | [global] variable_declaration`, and its <type_mark> production (lines ~35-38) is only `integer | float | string | bool`. There is no `<type_declaration>` production and no `enum` keyword anywhere in the 187-line spec text. The implementation nonetheless dispatches a full third declaration kind on T_TYPE (parse_base_declaration, parser.cpp:386-390/416-419, and parse_type_declaration, parser.cpp:1416-1474), and every parse_type_mark overload additionally accepts a bare identifier as a type mark (e.g. parser.cpp:710-718) and an elaborate `enum { id, id, ... }` construct (e.g. parser.cpp:719-817). This is grammar over-acceptance relative to the stated authoritative target: programs using `type ... is ...;` or `enum {...}` or `variable x : SomeOtherIdentifier;` are accepted as valid by this parser even though spec2023.txt's grammar does not sanction any of those forms. (Marked speculative because it is possible this functionality was carried over from a different course-year's grammar that did include these constructs, per the codebase's documented multi-year provenance, rather than being a pure implementation error against spec2023 specifically.)
findings.evidence: spec2023.txt (lines 42-46): `<declaration> ::= [ global ] <procedure_declaration> | [ global ] <variable_declaration>` -- no third alternative. spec2023.txt (lines 35-38): `<type_mark> ... integer | float | string | bool` -- no enum/identifier alternative. `grep -n -i "type_declaration\|enum" spec2023.txt` returns no grammar-rule matches. Implementation: parser.cpp:386-390 dispatches T_TYPE to parse_type_declaration; parser.cpp:710-718 and 719-817 (repeated in the other two parse_type_mark overloads at 908-916/918-1016 and 1075-1083/1085-1183) implement identifier-type-mark and enum handling not present in the grammar.

findings.title: parse_program()/parse_procedure_declaration() unconditionally overwrite the header sub-parse's boolean result
findings.description: `bool parser::parse_program()` computes `valid_parse = parse_program_header();` and then immediately overwrites it with `valid_parse = parse_program_body();` on the very next line, discarding the header's success/failure. The identical pattern occurs in `parse_procedure_declaration` (`valid_parse = parse_procedure_header(is_global); valid_parse = parse_procedure_body();`, parser.cpp:441-442). In practice the top-level 'parsed successfully'/'had parsing errors' message is driven separately by errors_occured plus the trailing-period check, so this does not currently produce a wrong final message, but the discarded return values are dead computations that could mask a genuine early failure being silently overridden by a later step's (possibly coincidental) success, and make the code's control flow misleading to readers/maintainers.
findings.evidence: parser.cpp:134-135 `valid_parse = parse_program_header(); valid_parse = parse_program_body();` and parser.cpp:441-442 `valid_parse = parse_procedure_header(is_global); valid_parse = parse_procedure_body();` -- in both cases the first assignment's value is never read before being replaced.

findings.title: parse_procedure_header continues parsing after a missing procedure-name identifier instead of returning, registering symbol-table entries under an empty procedure name
findings.description: When parse_procedure_header encounters a non-identifier where the procedure name is expected, it reports an error but (unlike almost every other error branch in this file) does not `return false;` -- it falls through with `procedure_name` left as the empty string `""`, then proceeds to parse `:` and the type mark via `parse_type_mark(procedure_name, 1)` and any parameter list via `parse_parameter_list(procedure_name)`, all keyed on the empty-string name. This routes add_procedure_valid_inputs/update_procedure_return_type calls at map[""] / scope_table[scope_id].scope_map[""], polluting the symbol table with an unnamed-procedure entry and potentially colliding with any other malformed declaration in the same scope that also falls through with an empty name.
findings.evidence: parser.cpp:479-490: the else-branch for missing identifier does `generate_error_report("Procedure must be named a valid identifier"); errors_occured = true; Current_parse_token = Get_Valid_Token(); //valid_parse = resync_parser(state); //return false;` -- both the resync and the return are explicitly commented out, so execution falls through to the T_COLON check and parse_type_mark(procedure_name, 1) at parser.cpp:500 with procedure_name == "".

notes:
Scope covered: parse_program/parse_program_header/parse_program_body (parser.cpp:129-358), parse_base_declaration (362-434), parse_procedure_declaration/header/body (436-678), all three parse_type_mark overloads (683-1191), parse_parameter_list/parse_parameter (1197-1233, 1528-1538), both parse_variable_declaration overloads (1238-1395), parse_bound/parse_number (1399-1411, 1541-1569), parse_type_declaration (1416-1474), update_scopes (3289-3302), update_context_token (3304-3316), resync_parser (2620-3287), and the declaration-writing SymbolTable.cpp methods (resync_tables, remove_scope, update_identifier_type, update_identifier_data_type, add_procedure_valid_inputs, update_procedure_return_type, make_token_global, get_globabl_token, token_is_in_global_scope).

Methodology: primarily static reading + control-flow tracing against parser.h/parser.cpp/SymbolTable.cpp/ScopeTable.cpp/token.h, cross-checked against spec2023.txt's grammar (program/program_header/program_body/declaration/procedure_header/procedure_body/parameter_list/parameter/variable_declaration/type_mark/bound productions, and the semantics section's numbered rules, notably rule 4 on global-name uniqueness/shadowing). For the highest-severity items I additionally built an isolated copy of the full source tree under the scratchpad directory (never touched the real repo — confirmed via `git status`/`git diff --stat` showing no tracked-file changes) and either (a) compiled with `g++ -O2 -Wall -Wextra` to surface `-Wmaybe-uninitialized` diagnostics, or (b) added temporary one-line debug prints in that scratch copy and ran crafted .src test programs through the built `./compiler` to directly observe symbol-table state and hang/CPU behavior. All such empirical results are quoted verbatim in the findings' evidence fields; the repo's own source files were never modified.

Not re-reported (already covered by the repo's own CLAUDE.md and independently visible but out of scope for "new" reporting per instructions): the SIGILL/-Wreturn-type crash family (Typechecker::second_relation_token_chains, Typechecker::check_return_statement, SymbolTable::create_new_scope_table missing returns), the stubbed check_assignment_statement, and the general "scope ids get reused by later sibling procedures" behavior (verified consistent with update_scopes' depth-based id scheme and remove_scope's proper table erasure — did not find this reuse itself to corrupt data beyond the separately-reported global-scope bugs).

Also investigated but not flagged as new bugs (checked and found working as intended): parameter registration scope (parameters are correctly written into the procedure's own — already-incremented — scope_id, not the parent's); procedure-name dual visibility (own scope + scope_id-1, via resync_tables' I_PROCEDURE special case) — matches the documented design.

All file paths referenced are under /datadrive/data/compiler-course/ (parser.cpp, parser.h, SymbolTable.cpp, SymbolTable.h, ScopeTable.cpp, ScopeTable.h, token.h). Spec citations are from /tmp/claude-1000/-datadrive-data-compiler-course/e0905122-5395-4b36-add9-f6a81e41bd28/scratchpad/spec-text/spec2023.txt.
